messages.subject: colwise(fun, .cols, process = c(“all”, “discrete”,”numeric”))
parts:
I wonder whether the functionality of catcolwise and numcolwise could usefully be rolled into colwise?

colwise(fun, .cols, process = c(“all”, “discrete”,”numeric”))

The default behavior would be unchanged for backward compatibility, but you could control its activity without learning a new function, and the abiltiy to control the application is discoverable from the parameter completion list.

Ideally .cols could take the process parameter,: but that would conflict with single columns called all, discrete or numeric :-)

Hi Tim,

Have you looked at the source code? ;)

numcolwise <- function (.fun, .try = FALSE) {
colwise(.fun, is.numeric)
}
catcolwise <- function (.fun, .try = FALSE) {
colwise(.fun, is.discrete)
}

Hi Hadley!

nifty! :-) Is there a reason not expose that in the help or the parameter list?

Mind if I ask two and half followup questions?

Question one: Is there a reason that qplot doesn’t optionally take a formula as an input in place of x, y?

I use formulae wherever they’re supported, and find it mildly awkward to switch from plot(y~x) to qplot(x,y) both because one’s not a formula, and the order is reversed.

y~x also gives a heads-up that this function demands a data.frame as input.

so qplot(DV ~IV, data=df) has a bounty from me of one wishlist book if delivered in time for christmas :-)

Extra bounty of a second book: allow this to work

y = x = 1:10
qplot(x,y) # i.e., if data == NULL, data = data.frame(x=x, y=y)

That would skip the step of making a fake df for a 1-off exploration

Question 2: If two or three parameters to one function are easier to learn than 2 or 3 functions, why not make a version of "applyr()" that has as parameters input.type = c(self, df, matrix, list, vector), out.type= c(slef, df, matrix, list, vector)?

Then people can learn one function call, and be explicit about what they expecting on the input and output side (rather than learning that the first two letters of the function name encode the data types taken an returned...


best, tim

parts: > nifty! :-) Is there a reason not expose that in the help or the parameter list?

Well, the docs say: " .cols: either a function that tests columns for
inclusion", which admittedly is a bit cryptic.

>
> Question one: Is there a reason that qplot doesn’t optionally take a formula as an input in place of x, y?
>
> I use formulae wherever they’re supported, and find it mildly awkward to switch from plot(y~x) to qplot(x,y) both because one’s not a formula, and the order is reversed.
>
> y~x also gives a heads-up that this function demands a data.frame as input.
>
> so qplot(DV ~IV, data=df) has a bounty from me of one wishlist book if delivered in time for christmas :-)
Basically I don't like the formula syntax because it doesn't extend naturally.

> Extra bounty of a second book: allow this to work
>
> y = x = 1:10
> qplot(x,y) # i.e., if data == NULL, data = data.frame(x=x, y=y)

> Question 2: If two or three parameters to one function are easier to learn than 2 or 3 functions, why not make a version of "applyr()" that has as parameters input.type = c(self, df, matrix, list, vector), out.type= c(slef, df, matrix, list, vector)?
>
> Then people can learn one function call, and be explicit about what they expecting on the input and output side (rather than learning that the first two letters of the function name encode the data types taken an returned...

That would obviously be fairly easy to do, but I haven't because:

* I think it's a generally a bad idea for function arguments to
determine the type of output - it makes the function harder to reason
about.

* Similarly, some argument only apply to some types of input/output,
so you'd need a whole lot of extra error handling to make sure the
user supplied the right arguments.

Hadley
